vectors.name: quote-tier-recovers-an-edited-block
vectors.note: The QUOTE tier's positive case, which the corpus had no normative vector for. vectors.name: quote-context-outranks-a-better-body-match
vectors.note: Ranking is by aggregate score, not by body score with context used only as a tiebreak afterwards. vectors.name: quote-near-duplicate-not-identical-commits-on-context-alone
vectors.note: The reachable near-duplicate hazard. Two byte-identical candidates that both differ from the quote, so their body scores are exactly equal (0.9358) and no body-score difference exists to decide between them: context is the whole reason one is chosen. The favoured candidate's raw aggregate is 1.0358, which the reported score clamps to 1.0, leaving a guarded margin of 0.0525 over the other twin's 0.9475. The corpus's other near-duplicate vector (near-dup-twins-detach-despite-high-score) is the identical-twin case, where both candidates reach 1.0 on body alone and the clamp leaves no margin at all. Here the id commits, which is what §9 permits when it allows up to 0.05 per side against a 0.05 margin.

vectors.name: quote-surviving-half-of-a-split-block-recovers
vectors.note: §9's split case: the block was cut in two and the quote is the whole original, so a surviving half is a strict substring of it. The half scores 2*20/(40+20) = 2/3, comfortably over the threshold, and recovers. This is the guarantee §9 describes when it says a surviving half must not 'score arbitrarily low'. Note that the containment floor §9 names for the job cannot be what delivers it: under containment the metric already returns 2s/(s+l), which exceeds the floor's s/l for every l > s, so the floor never raises a score. The guarantee holds; the named mechanism is inert.

vectors.name: quote-normalization-is-ascii-only
vectors.note: §9 folds ASCII case only, so 'CAFE' with an acute accent and its lowercase form are NOT the same string: they score 0.9412, not 1.0. vectors.name: marker-tier-lookup-does-not-hit-a-subhash-id
vectors.note: SPEC.md §16 mandatory reader rule (v1.6): a tool MUST NOT report a marker carrying the exact `subhash` key as the stay of the block containing it. The key is compared exactly, without segmenting or resolving a child, so a tool that implements neither §5.5 nor §5.6 still applies it. §9.2's MARKER tier looks the stay's id up in the after-document. `m1` appears there only as a row-style child marker on a list item, which is not a block stay, so the ladder falls through to QUOTE and lands on the edited paragraph (target 0). An unfiltered lookup returns method `marker` and target 1: a confident, silent bind to the wrong block, which is the failure §16 makes this rule mandatory for.

vectors.name: hash-tier-ignores-a-block-claimed-by-a-marker
vectors.note: SPEC.md §9.1 tier 2 (v1.11): a block claimed at a stronger tier has left the pool. `a`'s block was rewritten into `b`'s exact text and kept `a`'s marker; `b` lost its marker and survived verbatim. Two blocks now carry `b`'s hash, but one is claimed by `a` at tier 1, so exactly one unclaimed block has it and `b` commits there (hash, target 1). vectors.name: hash-tier-needs-the-hash-recorded-by-one-stay
vectors.note: SPEC.md §9.1 tier 2 (v1.11): the stored hash must have been recorded by exactly one stay. One block carried both `a` and `b`, so both recorded one hash; with the markers stripped the block survives verbatim and is the only one with that hash, which the v1.10 ladder committed both ids to by HASH. Tier 3 then finds both selecting that block with identical quotes, which one copy of the text cannot hold disjointly, so both detach (`contested`, each reporting its own score).
